newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Mix of deals and developments.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Mix of deals and developments.

text.p: Asian debt markets offered up a mix of instruments on Thursday, as per usual.
The Asian Development Bank launched a Taiwan dollar-denominated bond, its second such issue.
The 7.0 billion Taiwan dollar bond (about US$255 million) carries a semi-annual coupon of six percent and was launched at par to yield 17 basis points over the Taiwan government bond number 86-3.
Chinatrust Commercial Bank was lead manager and bookrunner.
The bond and its predecessor that was issued in August 1995 are designed to help internationalise the island's bond market and raise the international credibility of Taiwan's currency.
In other debt news, Bakrie Indonesia BV launched and closed a US$50 million Eurobond through lead manager Merrill Lynch Far East.
The 9.625 percent three-year bond was priced and re-offered at 99.732 to yield 9.73 percent, or 400 basis points over the 5-7/8 percent U.S. Treasury note due November 1999.
The notes are guaranteed by Bakrie Investindo, which owns part of Indonesian listed company Bakrie and Brothers.
South Korea's Nara Banking Corp launched a US$40 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue.

In August, CS First Boston (Europe) AG took a 20 percent stake in Nara to become the single biggest shareholder in the bank. The issue requires CS First Boston to retain at least a 19 percent share in the bank, while the JS Kim family, the second largest shareholder, must hold at least 13 percent.
The three-year certificates can be put after one year at 99.62 and after two years at 99.81.
They pay a margin of 50 basis points and an all-in return of 68 points if held until maturity.
In the loan market, Hong Kong's Lai Sun Development formally launched its HK$1.5 billion term loan. The three-year deal pays 160 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate.
Fees are 30 basis points for top-tier participants.

In the local currency bond markets, the spread between Hong Kong Monetary Authority Exchange Fund bills yields and HIBOR continues to widen as banks scoop up the bills in anticipation of the launch of the HKMA's Real Time Gross Settlement System on Monday.
The spread widened to 120-150 basis points, making the cost of holding paper for RTGS onerous, money market dealers complained. Earlier this year, that spread was closer to 30 basis points.
Pressure on government paper yields started as banks began accumulating the paper in anticipation of the RTGS launch.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has said that banks can use Exchange Fund bills and notes to obtain interest-free intraday liquidity by carrying out intraday repurchase transactions with the HKMA under the RTGS system.
Dealers said they fear that the spread between Exchange Fund instruments and HIBOR could widen further as banks rush to buy government paper before next week.
